cards.explanation: David opens with the LORD, telling Him he loves Him. He says, "I love You, O LORD, my strength." (Psalm 18:1). No enemies yet, no story yet, just love. I bet when you've just been rescued, the thank-you can't wait its turn, friends. The whole song comes after that one sentence.

The answer is that he takes refuge. David says, "My God is my rock, in whom I take refuge…" (Psalm 18:2). A rock is something you get behind when trouble comes. He's not just calling God strong, he's saying he runs to Him. And when you've been shoved to the back of a junk drawer for years, like I was, you really notice who you can run to.

The answer is True. David says, "I will call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised…" (Psalm 18:3). He doesn't tack it on at the end. He says it while he's talking about being saved from his enemies. Praise and rescue show up in the same sentence.

The answer is that he calls on the LORD for help. David says, "In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried to my God for help." (Psalm 18:6). The cords of death have encompassed him and the torrents of chaos have overwhelmed him, and his move is to call. That's the whole plan, friends. Sometimes the best plan is the shortest one.

The answer is from His temple. The verse says, "From His temple He heard my voice, and my cry for His help reached His ears." (Psalm 18:6). David's cry travels all the way to the LORD's ears. Nothing gets lost on the way.

The answer is anger. The verse says the mountains "…were shaken because He burned with anger." (Psalm 18:7). Not a little tremble, either. The earth shook and quaked, and the foundations of the mountains trembled. When the LORD moves, creation notices.

The answer is hailstones and coals of fire. David says, "…hailstones and coals of fire." (Psalm 18:12). Then he says it again in verse 13, as the LORD thunders from heaven and the voice of the Most High resounds. Hail and burning coals, together. Friends, nobody would call that a light drizzle.

The answer is False. David says, "He shot His arrows and scattered the foes; He hurled lightning and routed them." (Psalm 18:14). Scattered, routed, nobody holding the line. If your foes get scattered, they didn't stand their ground.

The answer is that He takes hold of David and draws him out of deep waters. David says, "He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters." (Psalm 18:16). The LORD takes hold of him. David doesn't climb out by himself. When the water's over your head, friends, you want a hand like that.

The answer is True. David says the LORD rescued him "…from my powerful enemy, from foes too mighty for me." (Psalm 18:17). He doesn't pretend he could have handled them. That's honest, and honest is a good place to start. I've never been too mighty for anything either, except maybe a cookie box.

The answer is delighted. David says, "He rescued me because He delighted in me." (Psalm 18:19). He doesn't say it was because he earned it that day, he says the LORD delighted in him. That's a nice reason to be rescued. I'll take it.

The answer is kept. David says, "For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God." (Psalm 18:21). Kept, held onto, didn't drop. Same word you'd use for a recipe you refuse to lose.

The answer is False. The verse says, "…to the pure You show Yourself pure, but to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd." (Psalm 18:26). The word is shrewd, not crooked. David uses that "but" to turn the line. The LORD isn't crooked.

The answer is those with haughty eyes. David says, "For You save an afflicted people, but You humble those with haughty eyes." (Psalm 18:27). Haughty eyes look down on others. The afflicted get saved, and the haughty get humbled.

The answer is that he can charge an army and scale a wall. David says, "For in You I can charge an army, and with my God I can scale a wall." (Psalm 18:29). Notice the "in You" and "…with my God…" He isn't saying he's tough, he's saying he's not alone. I couldn't charge an army, but I can scale a counter.

The answer is that it is flawless. David says, "As for God, His way is perfect; the word of the LORD is flawless." (Psalm 18:30). Flawless means there's nothing in it to fix. I've stamped thousands of cookies and never had a flawless one, so I notice that.

The answer is True. David asks, "For who is God besides the LORD? And who is the Rock except our God?" (Psalm 18:31). He doesn't wait for an answer, because the answer is none. It's a question that works like a statement. That's him saying there is no God besides the LORD.

The answer is that his arms can bend a bow of bronze. David says, "He trains my hands for battle; my arms can bend a bow of bronze." (Psalm 18:34). Bronze doesn't bend easily, and he says his arms can do it. The LORD does the training. I can barely bend a pipe cleaner.

The answer is the LORD's gentleness. David says, "You have given me Your shield of salvation; Your right hand upholds me, and Your gentleness exalts me." (Psalm 18:35). After bows and battles, the word he lands on is gentleness. I love that, friends. A strong hand that's also gentle.

The answer is broadens. David says, "You broaden the path beneath me so that my ankles do not give way." (Psalm 18:36). A wider path means fewer wobbles. I've been on a counter edge. I know the value of room.

The answer is True. David says, "I crushed them so they could not rise; they have fallen under my feet." (Psalm 18:38). This stretch of the song is heavy. I think it's okay to just let it be heavy, friends. It's what David says.

The answer is the LORD. David says, "You have armed me with strength for battle; You have subdued my foes beneath me." (Psalm 18:39). He's been saying "I" a lot in these verses, but here he gives the credit to the LORD. Strength and victory both come from Him. That's how David sings about it.

The answer is False. David says his enemies cried for help, and then the verse says "…but He did not answer." (Psalm 18:41). They called out, and no answer came. It's a heavy verse, and I think it's okay to say so, friends.

The answer is that they will serve him. David says, "a people I had not known shall serve me." (Psalm 18:43). A people he had not known will serve him. I think that's quite a turn. The LORD has made him head of nations.
The answer is cower. David says, "When they hear me, they obey me; foreigners cower before me." (Psalm 18:44). Cower means shrinking back. The same verse says they hear him and they obey.

The answer is above his foes. David says, "You exalt me above my foes; You rescue me from violent men." (Psalm 18:48). The LORD lifts him above his foes and rescues him from violent men. I think that's good news for David.

The answer is name. David says, "Therefore I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing praises to Your name." (Psalm 18:49). He sings to the LORD's name. And he plans to do it among the nations, out loud.

The answer is David and his descendants forever. The song ends, "Great salvation He brings to His king. He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever." (Psalm 18:50). Not just David, and not just for a while. The last word of the song is forever, friends.
